prompt: The client asks: "Should we buy a regional distributor for $80M?" Fact sheet: the distributor earns $10M a year from its other customers; owning it would also save us the $4M a year we pay it in fees; our hurdle is an 8-year payback; the distributor's owner is retiring; the distributor sponsors a local soccer team. Which is the best recommendation?

options.text: Don't buy. At $80M against $10M a year of earnings, payback is 8 years, right at the hurdle.
options.feedback: It leaves out the $4M a year of fees we'd stop paying, which bring payback under 6 years.

options.text: Buy it. It sponsors a local soccer team, which builds goodwill with customers across the region.
options.feedback: Sponsorship doesn't decide an $80M purchase. The payback does.

options.text: Buy the distributor: $10M from other customers plus $4M of fees saved repays the $80M in under 6 years.
options.feedback: Right. It leads with the answer and counts both sources of value without double counting.

options.text: The deal sits near the hurdle and the owner is retiring, so more diligence is needed before taking a view.
options.feedback: This never commits, even though payback is under 6 years against an 8-year hurdle.

explanation: Full answer: Buy the distributor. Its $10M from other customers plus the $4M of fees we'd stop paying gives a payback under 6 years on $80M, inside our 8-year hurdle; the $10M excludes business with us, so nothing is counted twice. The main risk is that key staff leave when the owner retires, so the next step is to secure retention agreements with the top managers before signing. What would change the answer: earnings from other customers below about $6M a year, which would push payback to 8 years.

irrelevant_facts: The distributor sponsors a local soccer team.
